analysis.title: AI Data Centers and the New Compute of Politics, Power and Capex
key_insights: The U.S. midterms crystallized the politics of data centers. Several newly elected governors campaigned on restricting development. Neuberger does not think this changes why the AI buildout is happening, but it changes how, where and how fast it proceeds.

Four dates matter: late 2026 permitting reform (the one major energy bill with bipartisan support and a realistic chance of passing before the new Congress takes office Jan. 3), December 10 Texas audit results, January/February Q4 earnings with 2027 capex guidance, and January onward new governors and legislatures (watch Texas, Ohio, Georgia).
The Texas audit on December 10 is expected to separate serious data center projects from speculative ones, which could speed up the serious ones.
Neuberger expects 2027 capex guidance to keep rising, but how companies discuss funding may matter as much as the number.

Hyperscalers are locking in land, buildings and power now and deciding on chips later, which leaves room to slow spending if demand weakens. If demand holds, capex estimates keep rising and free cash flow stays under pressure for one to two years.

Financing is now central for hyperscalers. One large cloud provider has raised roughly $115 billion of long-term debt this year and may consider selling equity, and another is raising about $98 billion of equity. More of this is expected ahead of Q4 earnings.
Operating cash flow is strong and backlogs are healthy. The bigger risk to hyperscalers is slowing cloud or other revenue growth, not a lack of funding.

Utilities: the key issues are who pays for new generation and transmission, whether electricity stays affordable, who is appointed to utility commissions, and how much proposed demand becomes signed contracts. The likeliest outcome is a middle ground in which data centers pay their own way, including by supplying some of their own power.

Texas downside for utilities is limited: the legislature is Republican, the Senate must confirm new utility commissioners, and the outgoing governor had already paused approvals, so scrutiny is bipartisan.

Utilities in Florida, Louisiana, Indiana, Missouri and Iowa look better placed to win new load than those in less receptive states such as Ohio. Signed long-term take-or-pay contracts should keep earnings steady.

Midstream: the case for gas pipelines rests on the need for reliable power, with utilities building gas plants again. FERC retains a 3-2 Republican majority, limiting near-term risk. Senate confirmation of future commissioners is the longer-term lever. Energy was the best-performing S&P 500 sector in both years of the last Democratic Congress (2021-2022).

Semiconductors carry more delay risk than the companies building data centers. Near-term demand is largely committed, but capacity is being planned for demand years out. If projects slip in states with large planned builds, particularly Texas and Ohio, oversupply becomes a risk for demand, pricing and profitability in 2028 and beyond.

Neuberger thinks some semiconductor risk is already priced in, with compressed valuations and weak stock performance. The long-term build is still expected to continue, but the industry is cyclical and digestion periods are possible.

Baseline is a high but more selective buildout. The view would turn more cautious on: hyperscaler signals of slowdown (lower 2027 capex guidance, stalling cloud growth, chipmaker order digestion), pauses becoming law (moratoriums surviving legal challenge, especially in Texas), punitive cost-sharing (new fees and taxes), or funding strains (wider credit spreads on AI debt, weak reception for equity raises).

Selectivity over direction: the buildout favors companies with strong balance sheets, signed contracts and a clear path through permitting. The next few quarters are a test of who is best placed within the AI trade, not a verdict on it.

sector_views.rationale: Politics affects cash flow through laws, regulatory decisions and permitting. Utilities in FL, LA, IN, MO and IA look better placed to win new load than those in Ohio. Take-or-pay contracts keep earnings steady where projects are signed.
Gas demand for reliable power is not partisan, utilities are building gas plants again, and FERC keeps a 3-2 Republican majority, limiting near-term risk.

More delay risk than data center builders and oversupply risk in 2028 and beyond if projects slip in Texas and Ohio. Some of this is priced in, and the long-term build is expected to continue, though the cycle may bring digestion.
Capex estimates keep rising and free cash flow stays under pressure for one to two years if demand holds. Financing is central. Main risk is slowing cloud revenue growth, not funding.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers are locking in land, buildings and power now, operating cash flow is strong, backlogs are healthy, and capex estimates keep rising. Permitting reform and a Texas audit that sorts out speculative projects could speed up serious ones.
tension_points.bear_case: Newly elected governors campaigned on restricting development, projects may slip on permitting or local opposition, and free cash flow stays under pressure for one to two years. Slipping projects in Texas and Ohio could cause chip oversupply in 2028 and beyond.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Lower 2027 capex guidance, stalling cloud growth, or order digestion at chipmakers; moratoriums that survive legislative and legal challenges in Texas; wider credit spreads on AI debt or a weak reception for equity raises.
